transcript:
"This is NPR News Now, the latest headlines every hour."
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Rylan Barton.
The Trump administration made a highly unusual court filing today about the U.S. Senate race
in Alaska.
They're asking a federal judge to block the certification of the election results if the
Republican candidate loses.
And today, President Trump told reporters he ordered the lawsuit.
NPR's Hansilo Wong reports.
Out of the four U.S. Senate candidates in Alaska, two have similar names — the sitting
senator Dan Sullivan, a Republican, and Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., who is not affiliated with
a local party.
Alaska's Republican Party supported an earlier lawsuit in state court that tried to stop
this.
But in June, the Alaska Supreme Court ruled that Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. has the right to
run as a candidate.
Now in a federal court filing, the Justice Department says that if Republican Senator
Dan Sullivan does not win, a judge should block Alaska from certifying the election
results.
The DOJ argues those results could be "impacted by voter confusion."
Many election law experts are skeptical of the Justice Department's argument, which
cites the preamble of the National Voter Registration Act.
Hansilo Wong, NPR News.
A bipartisan group of lawmakers is urging the Pentagon to immediately restore Ukraine's
access to the SpaceX Star Shield satellite Internet system used to intercept Russian drones.
Today, President Trump brushed off questions about the role SpaceX CEO Elon Musk played
in the disruptions.
Alexander Ward of the Wall Street Journal told NPR's Here and Now it's unclear who
ordered the service to be throttled.
SpaceX says the White House gave some sort of directive, implicit or explicit, to Musk
to do this.
The White House says Elon acted on his own, and now they're sort of working it out.
But that Elon also has the ability to do this because it's a private company.
But then the administration's messaging on this kind of changed yesterday.
Not only just Trump calling Musk to unthrottle the system, but you also had Vice President
J.D. Vance say, look, you know, Musk wouldn't have done this without some sort of input
from the U.S. government.
There's still a big mystery out there as to, did Musk go rogue, or was there some sort
of still White House green light?
Alexander Ward from the Wall Street Journal reporting, "The price of jet fuel climbed
to a new record high this week, and NPR's Joel Rose reports fuel costs are pushing holiday
air fares to some of their highest levels in years."
The average price for a gallon of jet fuel in the U.S. was $4.90 on Thursday, according
to the tracking firm Argus.
That's the highest single-day average the firm has ever recorded, and more than twice
what the average price was a year ago.
Fuel is one of airlines' biggest expenses, and they are paying billions of dollars more
for it than they did last year.
Carriers are absorbing some of those higher costs, according to the trade group Airlines
for America.
But they're also passing some of those costs on in the form of higher fares.
Air fares for Thanksgiving are up about 30 percent compared to last year, while ticket
prices for the Christmas holiday are up more than 20 percent.
Joel Rose, NPR News, Washington.
Major U.S. stock indexes fell today as the market came under increasing pressure from
rising oil prices.
The S&P 500 lost more than half a percent.
It's NPR.
French authorities are deploying 70,000 law enforcement officers nationwide to prevent
violence during planned protests tomorrow.
The move aims to avoid a repaint of last week's unrest.
Major Paris museums, including the Louvre, will be closed.
Demonstrators are protesting high living costs.
Last week's protests turned violent, with fires looting and clashes with police.
For generations, visitors to New York City have climbed into horse-drawn carriages for
postcard tours of Central Park.
Reporter Steve Kastenbaum says the city council has now voted to ban them.
People have been able to hire a horse-drawn carriage for a ride through the park since
1858.
If this ban survives legal challenges from the driver's union, the popular tourist attraction
will disappear in two years.
City Council President Julie Menon.
They don't belong in an area that attracts 42 million people a year, pulling a thousand
pound carriage in record-breaking heat.
New York's horse-drawn carriage industry supports around 150 drivers.
Under the legislation, the city would have to develop a transition plan to help them
find new jobs.
Several other cities have passed similar bans with the most recent one winning approval
in Philadelphia.
For NPR News, I'm Steve Kastenbaum in New York.
The Milwaukee Brewers and Tampa Bay Rays face off in a unique World Series starting tonight.
Both teams are seeking their first championship, and they both rely on a throwback style of
play focusing less on home runs.
Both teams also have modest payrolls, marking a big shift from big spending franchises.
I'm Rylan Barton, and from Washington, this is NPR News.

topics.text: Trump administration asks federal judge to block Alaska Senate election certification if Republican loses
Bipartisan lawmakers urge Pentagon to restore Ukraine's access to SpaceX Starshield satellite internet
Jet fuel prices hit record high, pushing Thanksgiving and Christmas air fares sharply higher
Major U.S. stock indexes fall as rising oil prices pressure the market
France deploys 70,000 officers nationwide ahead of planned protests over high living costs
New York City Council votes to ban horse-drawn carriages from Central Park
Milwaukee Brewers and Tampa Bay Rays open World Series, both seeking first championship
